passage:
Subject: Load testing before the clinic booking launch

Hi Sudha,

Thanks for walking us through the new launch date in today's meeting. I understand the pressure from the client, and I want the launch to succeed too.

I'm writing because I'm worried about one part of the plan: skipping the load test. Last month, during the pilot, the booking page froze for twenty minutes when about three hundred patients logged in at once. If that happens at a real clinic, people could miss appointments they urgently need.

Two options I think could work:
1. Launch on the new date with only two clinics, and add the rest after the test.
2. Keep the full launch, but move it by four days so I can run the test over the weekend.

I've attached the pilot logs. I'm happy to discuss either option tomorrow. If we go ahead without any test, I think I'd need to raise it with the quality lead, because patients are involved.

Best,
Ritu

qa.q: How long did the booking page freeze during the pilot?
qa.a: The booking page froze for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Ritu worried about?
qa.a: Ritu is anxious that without a load test the system could freeze and patients could miss appointments they urgently need.

qa.q: What makes Ritu's way of disagreeing effective?
qa.a: Ritu documents the concern with logs, offers two practical alternatives, and says Ritu would escalate only because patient safety is at stake.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sudha might feel pressured by the client but also respected, since the email gives thanks, offers solutions and attacks no one.

grounding: Shows a young employee documenting concerns about a manager's decision, offering alternatives and reserving escalation for a safety issue.

Okay, you asked what I did about the weekend shifts. I'm Ankita, and here's the honest version.

Last year Jasleen, my manager at the call centre, kept giving me and two others every Saturday. Her favourites never got one. I was furious. I nearly went straight to HR.

Then I thought: is this an ethics problem, or an unfairness problem? Nobody was being harmed or cheated. It was unfair, but I could try something first.

So I kept a simple record for six weeks: who worked which weekend. Then I asked Jasleen for ten minutes and showed her a rota where everyone did one Saturday a month. I said, "I think this would be fairer and keep people from burning out."

She was defensive for a day. Then she used most of my rota.

I'm saving my big fights for things that really matter. This one just needed a spreadsheet and a calm voice.

qa.q: For how many weeks did Ankita keep a record of weekend shifts?
qa.a: Ankita kept a record for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when the favourites never got a Saturday?
qa.a: Ankita felt furious and treated unfairly, and was tempted to go straight to HR.

qa.q: Why did Ankita decide not to go to HR first?
qa.a: Ankita judged it unfair but not an ethics or safety problem, so documenting it and offering an alternative rota made more sense.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have seen the proposed rota at first, and later?
qa.a: Jasleen was defensive for a day, perhaps feeling criticised, but then saw it was fair and adopted most of it.

grounding: Shows a young employee documenting an unfair manager decision, offering an alternative and choosing fights carefully rather than escalating at once.

At the agri-supplies shop by the Jalna bus stand, Deepak had given Dhruv his first job four years ago, when no one else would. Dhruv would have done almost anything for him.

In April a truck brought sacks of cotton seed left over from last season. Deepak tore off the old date stickers. "Tell the farmers it's the new batch. They won't know."

Dhruv felt sick. He knew these farmers. Old Kisan-kaka had bought seed from him for four seasons.

He waited until the shop was empty that evening. "Deepak-bhau, you gave me everything here. I'll work extra hours, whatever you need. But I can't tell them old seed is new. If it doesn't grow, they lose a whole season."

Deepak glared at him. Then he looked away. "So what do we do with forty sacks?"

"Label them honestly, sell them cheaper, and tell people why."

It took two days of silence before Deepak printed the new labels.

qa.q: How many sacks of old seed did the shop have?
qa.a: The shop had forty sacks of old seed.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when Deepak tore off the date stickers?
qa.a: Dhruv felt sick and torn, grateful and loyal to Deepak but troubled at the thought of deceiving farmers he knew.

qa.q: Which choice did Dhruv make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Dhruv refused to deceive the farmers while still offering loyalty and a practical alternative, honest labels at a lower price.

qa.q: Why might Deepak have been silent for two days?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt angry, embarrassed at being refused and worried about losses, before accepting the honest option.

grounding: Shows a young worker weighing loyalty to his manager against honesty and refusing to deceive customers.

Friday, 1 a.m.

I found out today. Ankita, my co-founder, my friend of eight years, has been moving our biggest clients to a new firm she registered in March. Siddharth, you idiot, I kept thinking, how did you not see it.

I've never been this angry. I wrote a long post naming her, with screenshots, ready to go. I wanted everyone in the industry to know. My finger was literally on the button.

Then I remembered Mr Rao's story, how he spent six years fighting an ex-partner and lost his health doing it.

So I saved the draft and closed the laptop. Instead I did three things: exported every email and invoice, changed the shared passwords, and booked a meeting with a lawyer for Monday.

I still hate what she did. I might hate her for a while. But I want my company and my life back, not a six-year war.

Going to try to sleep.

qa.q: When had Ankita registered the new firm?
qa.a: Ankita registered the new firm in March.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling with a finger on the button to post?
qa.a: Siddharth felt enraged and betrayed, wanting everyone in the industry to know what Ankita had done.

qa.q: What calm steps did Siddharth take instead of posting, and why do they help?
qa.a: Exporting emails and invoices, changing passwords and booking a lawyer protect the company and work through proper channels instead of revenge.

qa.q: What lesson from Mr Rao's story shaped Siddharth's choice?
qa.a: Mr Rao spent six years fighting an ex-partner and lost his health, showing how revenge can consume years.

grounding: Shows a young founder enraged by a partner's betrayal choosing documented, legal and calm steps instead of destroying her reputation.

People ask if I hate Yusuf. I'm Kalyani, by the way, and no, I don't. I did for a while.

We started the tuition centre together at twenty-three. By year three, he was taking the classes he liked and leaving me the accounts, the parents' complaints, everything. When I raised it, he said I was "too controlling". That stung for months.

Last year we decided to end it. We sat down with a friend who's a chartered accountant and wrote everything out: who keeps the name, who keeps which batches, how the savings are split. We signed it. No shouting.

The day he moved his last box out, I made him tea. It felt strange, but also light.

What I kept is the lesson, not the bitterness. My new partner and I wrote our roles on paper before we opened. And when I see Yusuf at the market, I say hello and mean it.

qa.q: Who helped Kalyani and Yusuf write out the terms?
qa.a: A friend who's a chartered accountant helped them.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling on the day Yusuf moved his last box out?
qa.a: Kalyani felt it was strange but also light, a sense of relief and letting go.

qa.q: Which choices helped Kalyani let go of bitterness?
qa.a: Ending the partnership with clear written terms, making tea on the last day, and keeping only the lesson by defining roles with a new partner.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Kalyani's hello at the market?
qa.a: Yusuf might feel relieved and respected, since there is no hostility left between them.

grounding: Shows a young business owner ending a partnership with clear terms and letting go of bitterness while keeping the lesson.

I run the front desk at the yoga studio Sumit and Nandini opened together, so I saw most of it.

For a year they argued about everything: the schedule, the new branch, who spent what. Nandini had quietly taken the morning batch with her when she started teaching at another studio. Sumit found out from a student.

He was angry for weeks. He'd slam the register drawer. I was sure it would end in court.

Instead, one Sunday they sat in the empty studio with a lawyer and a printed list. I brought them water. I couldn't hear much, but I saw Sumit read the list twice and sign it. The studio would stay his; Nandini would keep her own students.

As she left, Sumit held the door for her. "Good luck with it," he said. I don't know what he felt inside. But the next week he put a new rule on the board: every teacher's contract in writing.

qa.q: What did Sumit put on the board the next week?
qa.a: Sumit put up a new rule: every teacher's contract in writing.

qa.q: What did Sumit's slamming of the register drawer suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggested Sumit was angry and hurt after learning from a student that Nandini had taken the morning batch.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped him move on well?
qa.a: He ended the partnership with clear written terms, wished Nandini well, and turned the lesson into a new rule instead of holding on to bitterness.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when Sumit held the door and wished her luck?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt relieved and surprised, since the anger she expected did not come.

grounding: Shows a young business partner ending a partnership on clear terms and letting go of bitterness while keeping the lesson.

"We lost the school uniform contract," Sonali said, dropping into her chair. "To Nidhi Garments. Again."

Irawati looked up from the sewing machine. "What did they have that we didn't?"

"They're just lucky."

"Are they? Let's find out. Call the school and ask. Politely."

Sonali made a face, but she called. She came back twenty minutes later. "They sent a full sample kit, every size, before the meeting. And they promised delivery in three weeks. We said six."

"Three weeks." Irawati whistled. "How?"

"The principal said they cut and stitch in batches by size, not by order."

"Okay. So they taught us something for free."

Sonali laughed. "Fine. Sample kits for the next tender. And we try batching the collars next month."

"And we send Nidhi Garments a congratulations message."

"That's too much."

"It's not. We'll be competing with them for years."

When Samir's catering company won the Kulkarni wedding over us, I sulked for two days. I'm Vikas, and I'd been sure the menu we offered was better.

Then I did something my old boss used to do: I called the client and asked, honestly, why. The bride's father was kind about it. "Samir's team invited us for a tasting. And they sent a message every week with updates. We never had to chase them."

That stung, because both were easy. We just hadn't thought of them.

So the next month we started free tastings on Saturdays and a weekly update message for every booked family. I even sent Samir a short note: "Congratulations on the Kulkarni wedding. Your tastings are a smart idea."

He replied with a thumbs up and, a week later, sent us a client whose date he couldn't take. We're rivals. We're also, it turns out, each other's best teachers.

qa.a: Samir's team invited the family for a tasting and sent weekly update messages.

When Madhav opened a new sweet shop across the square in Karad, he took most of the Diwali box orders in his first year.

Hrithik, whose family shop had stood there for forty years, couldn't stop watching. He counted Madhav's customers from behind his own counter. He told anyone who would listen that Madhav used cheap ghee. None of it was true, and he knew it.

Meanwhile the jalebis in his own shop went soggy because nobody minded the oil. A regular customer, Shobha-tai, returned a box of stale pedhas. Hrithik barely noticed.

His father noticed. One evening he sat Hrithik down. "Your grandfather never once talked about another shop. He talked about his sweets." He placed the returned box on the counter. "You're losing our customers yourself."

Hrithik stared at the box for a long time. The next morning he stood at the frying pan himself, and he stopped saying anything at all about Madhav.

qa.a: Shobha-tai returned a box of stale pedhas.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he counted Madhav's customers?
qa.a: Hrithik felt jealous and resentful, obsessed with the rival's success.

qa.q: What went wrong for Hrithik, and what did he do to fix it?
qa.a: Spreading false rumours and watching the rival made him neglect his own sweets and lose customers; he returned to the frying pan and stopped talking about Madhav.

qa.q: How does Hrithik's father see what is happening?
qa.a: His father sees that the obsession with Madhav, not Madhav himself, is costing the family shop its customers.

grounding: Shows how a young shop owner's hatred of a rival leads him to spread negativity and lose customers, and how he turns back to his own work.

passage:
At the playground in Valparaíso, eighteen-month-old Emil headed straight for the tall slide, and his mother, Camila, felt her heart jump into her throat.

She had never known love like this, or fear like this. Some nights she stood by his cot just to hear him breathe.

"No, Emil! Come here!" she called, and grabbed his arm harder than she meant to. He burst into tears.

Camila knelt down. Her own hands were shaking. "I'm sorry. I got scared and I pulled too hard. That wasn't okay."

Emil sniffed and pointed at the slide again.

She took a breath. "Okay. The little slide first. I'll stay right here." She stood at the bottom, arms ready but not holding, as he climbed three steps, then slid down laughing.

He did it eleven times. Each time she let go a little more.

qa.q: How many times did Emil go down the slide?
qa.a: Emil went down the slide eleven times.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when Emil headed for the tall slide?
qa.a: Camila felt a rush of fear alongside intense love, her heart jumping into her throat.

qa.q: How did Camila repair after grabbing Emil's arm?
qa.a: She knelt, apologised, named that she got scared and pulled too hard, and then guided him to a safer slide instead of stopping him completely.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have been like for Emil if Camila had kept pulling him away?
qa.a: Emil might have felt frightened and blocked from exploring, instead of gaining confidence while his mother stayed close.

grounding: Shows a young mother feeling intense love and fear, learning to guide rather than control, and repairing after losing patience.

The waiting room at the child health clinic was full, and two-year-old Hansa had decided she would not sit still.

Tushar held her on his lap and felt the familiar mix: so much love it almost hurt, and a fear he couldn't name. Every cough from another child made him pull her closer.

Hansa wriggled free and ran for the fish tank. "Hansa, sit!" he snapped, louder than he meant. The other parents looked up. Hansa's lip trembled.

Tushar felt ashamed. He went over and crouched beside her. "Papa shouted. I'm sorry. I was worried and tired." She touched his cheek.

"Can you show me the orange fish?" he asked. She pointed. He stayed crouched next to her, letting her choose which fish to show him next, until the nurse called her name.

A grandmother nearby smiled at him. "Good that you said sorry," she said. "They remember that."

qa.q: What did Hansa run towards in the waiting room?
qa.a: Hansa ran towards the fish tank.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when the other parents looked up?
qa.a: Tushar felt ashamed of snapping, on top of the worry and tiredness he already felt.

qa.q: What small step helped Tushar repair with Hansa?
qa.a: He crouched, apologised in simple words and then followed her lead with the fish, guiding her gently instead of controlling her.

qa.q: How does the grandmother nearby see Tushar's apology?
qa.a: She sees it as a good example, saying children remember when a parent says sorry.

grounding: Shows a young father feeling intense love and fear, snapping at his toddler and repairing, learning to guide rather than control.

"Hemant! I told you not to carry the juice to the sofa!" Deepika shouted.

Hemant, five, froze with the empty cup. Orange juice was spreading across the cushion.

"Why can't you ever listen?" she said, even louder.

His eyes filled. He dropped the cup and ran to his room.

Deepika stood there, breathing hard. She had been up at five with a work deadline. She sat on the floor for a minute and counted her breaths. Then she knocked on his door.

"Can I come in?"

"No."

"Okay. I'll sit here." She sat outside. "Hemant, I shouted. That was not okay. I was tired and cross, and I took it out on you. I'm sorry."

The door opened a crack. "You were really loud."

"I was. Next time I'm cross, I'll stop and take three breaths first. Will you help me remember?"

He nodded. "And I'll carry juice to the table."

qa.a: Hemant was five.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling as she sat on the floor counting her breaths?

This morning I snapped at Madhuri. I'm writing it down so I remember what I did afterwards, not only the snapping.

We were late. Madhuri, who is four, wanted to wear her rain boots on a sunny day and cried when I said no. I said, "Amala has no time for this!" and pulled the boots off her feet. She went completely quiet in the auto. That silence was worse than crying.

All day at the office I felt heavy. I kept thinking I'm the kind of mother I promised I'd never be.

At bedtime I sat on her bed. "Madhuri, this morning Amala was angry and pulled your boots off. I'm sorry. Next time I'm rushing, I'll tell you I'm feeling hurried and we'll decide together."

She thought about it. "Can I wear them tomorrow?"

"If it's not muddy, yes."

She hugged my arm. I'm Dolma, I'm twenty-five, and I'm still learning.

passage:
When Nanaji died after two years in bed, Uma didn't cry at the funeral. She stood in the Lucknow house handing out water, and felt nothing at all.

At night came other feelings, one after another. Anger at the doctors, then at herself for not visiting more. And one she was ashamed of: relief. No more hospital runs, no more watching him struggle.

"Is something wrong with me?" she asked her husband Abhinav on the fourth night. "I feel relieved."

Abhinav sat beside her. "You loved him and you watched him suffer. Relief makes sense. It doesn't cancel the love."

She kept every ritual with her mother: the lamp each evening, the thirteenth-day prayers. Her friends kept calling. Some days she was fine; some days she wasn't.

Three months later, hearing his favourite old song in a shop, Uma finally cried, standing in the aisle. It felt like the grief had simply arrived on its own timetable.

qa.q: After how many years in bed did Nanaji die?
qa.a: Nanaji died after two years in bed.

qa.q: What did Uma feel that made her ask whether something was wrong with her?
qa.a: Uma felt relief that his suffering was over, and she felt ashamed and guilty about it.

qa.q: What helped Uma through her grief?
qa.a: Abhinav's reassurance that all her feelings were normal, keeping the rituals with her mother, friends' calls and allowing a long timeline.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see Uma's feeling of relief?
qa.a: Abhinav sees it as natural after watching someone suffer, and believes it doesn't cancel her love.

grounding: Shows a young woman grieving her grandfather through numbness, anger, guilt and relief, keeping rituals and support over a long timeline.

"You haven't said a word since the cremation," Anand said, sitting next to his brother on the terrace.

Lokesh kept staring at the water tank. "I'm angry."

"At who?"

"At Papa. For not going to the doctor sooner. At myself for not making him. And I'm angry that I'm angry. What kind of son is angry at his dead father?"

Anand was quiet for a moment. "The normal kind. I've been numb for five days. I keep waiting to cry and nothing comes."

"Is that normal?"

"Our pandit said grief doesn't come in order. It just comes."

Lokesh let out a long breath. "I can't do the thirteenth-day rituals alone."

"You won't. We'll do them together. And after that, we'll keep talking. Every Sunday, for as long as it takes."

Lokesh leaned his shoulder against his brother's. "Okay. Every Sunday."

qa.q: Where were Lokesh and Anand sitting?
qa.a: Lokesh and Anand were sitting on the terrace.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling after the cremation?
qa.a: Lokesh felt angry at his father and at himself, and guilty about being angry.

qa.q: How did Anand help Lokesh cope?
qa.a: Anand shared his own numbness, reassured Lokesh that different feelings are normal, and promised to do the rituals together and keep talking every Sunday.

qa.q: What is grief like for Anand?
qa.a: Anand feels numb and keeps waiting to cry, but nothing comes.

grounding: Shows young brothers grieving their father with anger and numbness, accepting each feeling as normal, keeping rituals and support.

passage:
After Zanele's mother died, the house in Durban filled with relatives who sang and cried late into the night. Zanele cried most of all, on the couch, in the kitchen, in the car.

Her husband Tariq didn't cry once. He fixed the dripping tap. He sorted out the chairs for the memorial. He cleaned the gutters on a Sunday.

On the sixth day Zanele snapped. "Don't you care? She loved you like a son."

Tariq put down the spanner. His voice shook. "I care. When my father died, I couldn't cry either. I fixed things. It's the only way I can hold it."

Zanele sat down on the step beside him. She had never seen that before.

After that, she didn't ask him to cry. She sang, and he mended the fence. Sometimes, when she was singing, he came and sat close without saying anything.

qa.q: What did Tariq clean on a Sunday?
qa.a: Tariq cleaned the gutters on a Sunday.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when she snapped at Tariq on the sixth day?
qa.a: Zanele felt hurt and alone in her grief, believing Tariq didn't care because he wasn't crying.

qa.q: What changed once Zanele understood Tariq's way of grieving?
qa.a: She stopped judging him for not crying, and they supported each other in their different styles, sometimes sitting close together.

qa.q: How does Tariq experience grief?

In the family room at the hospice, after Ammamma died at dawn, the cousins sat in a row of plastic chairs.

Gautam was crying openly, wiping his face with his sleeve. Next to him, Pema sat very straight, answering her phone, making lists of who to call, and asking the nurse about the papers.

"How can you be so calm?" Gautam said. It came out sharper than he meant.

Pema kept her eyes on the list. "Someone has to call Chennai."

The hospice counsellor, sitting nearby, spoke gently. "People grieve in different ways. Some cry. Some organise. Both can be love."

Gautam looked at Pema's hands. They were trembling on the pen.

"Sorry," he said. "Give me half the list. I'll call the Bengaluru relatives."

She passed it to him without a word. A few minutes later, she let her head rest on his shoulder, and for the first time that morning, she cried.

qa.q: Which relatives did Gautam offer to call?
qa.a: Gautam offered to call the Bengaluru relatives.

qa.q: What did Pema's trembling hands suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggested Pema was deeply sad and shaken, holding her grief in by organising.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that helped them support each other?
qa.a: He apologised for his sharp remark and took half the list, sharing the work and making space for Pema's grief.

qa.q: How did Gautam first see Pema's calmness, and how did that change?
qa.a: At first Gautam saw it as coldness, but after the counsellor's words and her trembling hands, he understood it was her way of grieving.

grounding: Shows young relatives learning to support each other's different grieving styles rather than judging who cries more.
